Simon — thanks for the clear asks and the sheet. Recap from our side and proposed next steps so your team can share internally: 

1) Core test matrix (what we’ll validate):
   - Baseline per-1M token run: 1M tokens across a representative chat mix (prompt+response avg tokens).
   - Batching sensitivity: run with batch sizes {1, 4, 8} and measure p50/p95 latency and throughput.
   - Cache hit simulation: replay dataset with cache-hit targets {0%, 25%, 50%} to observe token savings and latency variance.
   - Model variant fallback: compare Redwood-verified base model vs a smaller quantized variant for cost/latency tradeoffs.

2) Quick economics (initial conservative numbers to set expectations):
   - Redwood hosted (mixed chat): ~USD 40 per 1M tokens baseline. With moderate batching (batch=4) expect down to ~USD 30–32 per 1M.
   - Hyperscaler managed endpoints (typical managed GPU endpoint stack): ~USD 80–110 per 1M for equivalent latency SLOs in public benchmarks — depends on instance sizing/throughput.
   - Cache effects: a 25–40% cache hit rate typically reduces net token spend by ~15–30% depending on reply sizes.

Notes: these are ballpark estimates to help procurement prioritize — we’ll refine after the synthetic runs. Factors that move the numbers: payload size, average generation length, and whether you rely on longer context KV caching (which benefits Redwood’s runtime).

3) Proposed test ownership and timeline:
   - Redwood provides: test harness (k6 scripts + simple replay loader), a one-page runbook, and a pre-filled results spreadsheet template. (See attachment: redwood-vs-hypercaller-costs-1m-snapshot.pdf)
   - Stratus runs: synthetic workload and one live sample replay for cache-hit simulation.
   - Goal: run in your staging cluster over 3 business days, then a 2-day results consolidation. Target finish: 2026-10-22.

Next steps / asks for you: please confirm staging contact (SRE lead) and whether we should include your procurement on the kickoff. We’ll schedule a short 30-min kickoff to align test parameters.

Cheers,

Simon / Vanessa — adding a technical test plan and a few notes on measurement so results are actionable. Quick bullets, followed by the test matrix I’ll attach to the drive link: 

Measurement guidelines:
- Tokens: measure both input and output tokens; report normalized "billable tokens" per model definition.
- Latency: capture p50/p95/p99 per-request and also single-token generation latency where possible (helps interpret batching impact).
- Throughput: steady-state qps sustained for 10 minutes at each batch size to avoid warmup bias.
- Cost extrapolation: we’ll convert GPU runtime to token cost using our internal token/sec baselines so you get a direct $/1M token number.

Test matrix (high level):
- Run A (baseline): batch=1, model=redwood-mix-120B (non-quant), cache 0% — measure cost and latency.
- Run B (batching): batch=4, same model — expect ~20–30% lower token cost/sec in our runtime; latency p95 should increase but remain within most app SLOs if your p95 target >= 250ms.
- Run C (high batching): batch=8 — stronger throughput improvements, p95 may exceed tight interactive SLOs.
- Run D (quantized): smaller quantized variant — ~25–40% lower cost, small delta in output quality; include small eval prompt set for QA.
- Run E (cache replay): replay production-analogue with target cache_hits {0,25,50}. Measure net token delta and effective cost.

Ballpark numbers (after internal consolidation):
- Redwood baseline: USD 40 / 1M tokens. With batch=4 -> USD 30 / 1M. With batch=8 -> USD 24 / 1M.
- Hyperscaler managed endpoint (comparable latency tier): USD 85–100 / 1M (depends on instance family + reserved discounts).
- Quantized model on Redwood Dedicated/private: USD 18–22 / 1M depending on utilization and batch.

Caveats: hyperscaler numbers often look better if you accept higher latency or asynchronous batching or use lower-availability spot instances — we’ll explicitly model those permutations if you want.

I’ve uploaded a runnable k6 + python replay bundle to the shared Drive folder and a sample results workbook that computes the $/1M token using each run’s token counts and runtime. Link above.

If Stratus wants, we can run a jointly-observed run (Redwood runs against our hosted instance while Stratus runs against their hyperscaler lane) and compare side-by-side. That usually removes measurement variance.

— Ben
